what_it_does: RowHammer is a hardware vulnerability in modern memory chips (DRAM — the main working memory in a computer) where repeatedly reading one row of memory cells too quickly causes neighboring rows to flip their stored bits, which can be exploited by attackers. Memory manufacturers added a defense called DRFM (Directed Refresh Management) that tells the memory chip to refresh vulnerable rows, but the way DRFM is implemented today forces 8 to 32 memory banks to pause at the same time, causing up to 49% slowdowns in programs that access memory heavily. This paper proposes DREAM, a pair of smarter strategies: one batches together refresh commands from many banks so the shared pause does useful work for all of them at once, and another groups randomly chosen rows across banks under a single shared counter, dramatically cutting the bookkeeping storage needed. The goal is to get strong RowHammer protection without the performance penalty that current fixes impose.
